extracted.intended_audience: law professors, patent litigators, judges, and policy makers interested in patent remedies and empirical IP research
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical study and doctrinal analysis of how district courts have applied eBay's four-factor equitable test for permanent injunctions in patent litigation during the 7.5 years after eBay, including how factors like PAE status, technology field, and forum affect outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: eBay four-factor test
rubrics_metrics.description: After eBay v. MercExchange, district courts must apply a four-factor equitable test before granting permanent injunctive relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article treats eBay as replacing the prior 'general rule' of automatic injunctions and analyzes how courts apply the four factors in practice. The four typical factors (as applied in patent cases) are: (1) whether the plaintiff has suffered an irreparable injury; (2) whether remedies available at law, such as monetary damages, are adequate to compensate for that injury; (3) whether, considering the balance of hardships between the plaintiff and defendant, a remedy in equity is warranted; and (4) whether the public interest would not be disserved by a permanent injunction. The Article examines district court findings under each factor (see Parts V.A.6 and V.A.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-eBay presumption of injunctive relief for patentees
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, courts granted injunctive relief in the vast majority of patent cases upon findings of infringement and validity; a 'presumption' that prevailing patentees are entitled to injunctions existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article contrasts this historical dominance of property-rule remedies with eBay's rejection of a categorical rule. It cites Chief Justice Roberts' concurrence noting courts have granted injunctive relief since at least the early 19th century and explains how eBay represented a shift away from that presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreparable harm (prerequisite to injunction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff must demonstrate irreparable injury as a prerequisite to obtaining a permanent injunction under the eBay test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article emphasizes that PAEs frequently cannot establish the type of injury courts deem 'irreparable' post-eBay. It cites the district court’s post-remand MercExchange finding that willingness to license, lack of commercial activity, and public statements can rebut irreparable harm. The study analyzes courts' irreparable-harm findings (Part V.A.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of remedies at law (monetary damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts evaluate whether monetary damages (remedies at law) are adequate to compensate the patentee, as part of the eBay four-factor test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article examines how courts treat damages adequacy—e.g., where monetary relief may be inadequate because the patentee's exclusionary right is unique or hard to value. It connects this inquiry to debates over property vs. liability rules and valuation difficulties in IP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of hardships
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts weigh the hardship to the patentee of denying an injunction against the hardship to the defendant of granting one, as part of the eBay test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article considers how balance-of-hardships findings reflect factors like the defendant’s sunk costs, product-wide effects from enjoining a small component, and potential holdup concerns. These considerations are discussed among 'other eBay factors' (Part V.A.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an injunction would disserve the public interest is the fourth eBay factor courts must consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article discusses public-interest considerations in injunction decisions (e.g., public health when pharmaceuticals are at issue) and how this factor can weigh against injunctive relief in some technology contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee business model / PAE status (operating company vs non-practicing entity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patentee actively practices the patented technology (operating company) or principally enforces/licences patents (PAE/NPE) is a key predictor of injunction outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article finds a de facto bifurcated regime: operating companies that compete against an infringer still obtain injunctions in the vast majority of litigated-to-judgment cases, whereas PAEs and non-practicing patentees are generally denied injunctive relief. The study controls for technology field and forum and finds this effect robust (Part V.A.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition between litigants
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patentee and defendant compete in the same product market (i.e., patentee practices the patent in competition with the infringer) influences injunction grant rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article analyzes 'Grant Rate and Competition Between Litigants' (Part V.A.5), showing greater likelihood of injunctions where direct competition exists, consistent with commentators who argue for presumptive relief for competing patentees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of patented technology
rubrics_metrics.description: The technological field of the patented invention (e.g., pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, computer software) significantly affects injunction grant rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article reports nearly always granted injunctions for drugs and biotech patents but much less often for software. It treats 'Grant Rate by Patented Technology' as a central dimension of analysis (Part V.A.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum / district variation
rubrics_metrics.description: The particular district court (forum) in which the injunction request is decided affects grant rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study shows significant variation by district even after controlling for the propensity of PAEs to file in particular courts (Part V.A.3). The Article lists the dataset of decisions by district in Appendix A and discusses forum effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to license
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee's willingness to license broadly is a factor that can rebut claims of irreparable harm and weigh against injunctive relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned in the concurrences in eBay and in the district court's post-remand opinion in MercExchange, willingness to license has been used by courts to deny injunctions (e.g., evidence of licensing behavior, lack of exclusivity). The Article examines correlations between licensing behavior and injunction outcomes (Part V.A.8 discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of patented coverage within an accused product (small-component issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patented technology covers only a small component of a larger accused product is a consideration that may weigh against granting a product-wide injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article assesses whether courts treat patents covering small components as poorer candidates for injunctions, especially where an injunction would have disproportionate effects on the defendant’s product and third parties (discussed as one of the 'other eBay factors').

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding that the defendant willfully infringed the patent may influence the equitable decision to grant an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article examines whether willfulness findings correlate with injunction grants; courts and commentators have proposed willfulness as a factor supporting injunctive relief (discussed among eBay concurrences and in Part V.A.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Holdup and royalty-stacking concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: The risk that an injunction threat enables a patentee to extract royalties far above the patent’s ex ante value (holdup), or that cumulative royalties across multiple patents become excessive (royalty stacking), is a normative criterion motivating liability-rule preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article situates eBay within the larger literature debating property vs. liability rules and cites scholarship arguing holdup and royalty-stacking justify more reluctance to grant injunctions in certain contexts (e.g., standard-essential patents, complex products). It also cites empirical and theoretical critiques of the holdup hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of valuing patent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and scholars consider the inherent difficulty of valuing unique IP assets when deciding whether monetary damages are adequate—this supports property-rule reasoning for injunctions in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article explains this rationale for property rules: because IP assets are unique and hard to value (especially in fast-evolving industries), injunctions have historically been favored as the dominant remedy. It juxtaposes this with liability-rule arguments when valuation or transaction costs counsel otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of compulsory licensing / statutory liability rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory compulsory licensing provisions are examples of liability-rule regimes where infringement can be allowed in exchange for predetermined payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article notes Copyright Act examples (17 U.S.C. §§ 111, 114, 115) to illustrate liability-rule mechanisms and to frame doctrinal alternatives to injunctive relief in IP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall grant rate (dataset metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: The percentage of contested permanent injunction requests granted by district courts over the study period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article’s empirical analysis begins with an 'Overall Grant Rate' metric (Part V.A.1) as a baseline descriptive statistic for measuring eBay's impact. This metric is used in subsequent subgroup comparisons and regression analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant rate by PAE status (dataset metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison of injunction grant rates between PAEs (NPEs) and practicing patentees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article’s 'Grant Rate by PAE Status' (Part V.A.4) operationalizes PAE classification and quantifies the large difference in injunction outcomes between PAEs and operating companies, controlling for other variables in regression analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant rate by patented-technology (dataset metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Injunction grant rates broken down by technology field of the asserted patents (e.g., biotech, pharma, software).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article’s 'Grant Rate by Patented Technology' (Part V.A.2) shows differential treatment across tech sectors and discusses normative and doctrinal reasons for these differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant rate by district (dataset metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Injunction grant rates broken down by federal district court forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article’s 'Grant Rate by District' (Part V.A.3) documents significant forum variation and explores whether variation remains after controlling for litigant type and technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression analysis (statistical control of covariates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of multivariate regression to control for confounding variables (technology field, district, PAE status, competition, etc.) to isolate predictors of injunction grant outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article conducts regression analysis (Part V.A.8) to test the robustness of descriptive findings and to estimate the independent effect of factors such as PAE status and competition on likelihood of injunction grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreparable-harm evidentiary indicators (what courts cite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of evidence courts cite when making irreparable-harm findings (e.g., commercial activity, willingness to license, market competition, uniqueness of patented feature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article catalogues the kinds of factual findings courts rely on to find (or reject) irreparable harm and uses those as coding variables in the decisions dataset (Part V.A.6). Examples include MercExchange’s post-remand findings about licensing and commercial activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional indicators of patent value (patents dataset metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly accepted measures or proxies for patent value (used in the Article’s second dataset) and whether they predict injunction outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article’s second dataset explores whether indicators traditionally used to measure patent importance/value (discussed in Part V.B) correlate with injunction decisions; surprisingly, it finds such indicators are not predictive of injunction likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological transparency: study design, data collection, and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit research-questions-driven study design, data-collection procedures, coding rules, and acknowledgement of study limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part IV lays out 'RESEARCH QUESTIONS,' 'STUDY DESIGN AND DATA COLLECTION,' and 'LIMITATIONS' (Parts IV.A–C). The Article emphasizes coding decisions, the 7.5-year post-eBay window, and limits such as selection effects and generalizability — important criteria for assessing the empirical validity of findings.
